full_text: 659 Editorial EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 10 – 2026 After Regional Committee 73, what changes in health care for people in the Eastern Mediterranean Region? Adham Ismail1 1Officer-in-Charge, WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, Cairo, Egypt. Keywords: health financing, financial protection, universal health coverage, multi-communicable disease elimination, health system resilience, health equity, Eastern Mediterranean Citation: Ismail A. After Regional Committee 73, what changes in health care for people in the Eastern Mediterranean Region? East Mediterr Health J. 2026;32(10):659–661. https://doi.org/10.26719/2026.32.10.659. Copyright © Authors 2026. EMHJ is an open-access journal. This paper is available under the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 IGO licence (CC BY 3.0 IGO; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/igo). Meeting in Cairo from 13 to 15 October 2026 for the 73rd Session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Eastern Mediterranean (RC73), health ministers adopted 2 resolutions that could fundamentally change how countries finance health care and tackle communicable diseases across the Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR). The scale of health needs stands in stark contrast to the resources available to meet them. The EMR is home to just 9% of the world’s population, yet almost half of all people requiring humanitarian assistance live here. The region accounts for less than 2% of the global health spending (1). As of the end of June 2026, 48 disease outbreaks were active across 17 EMR countries and territories, including cholera, measles, dengue, malaria, and vaccine-derived poliovirus (1). Between July 2025 and June 2026, some 632 attacks on health care were recorded, causing 1531 deaths – 86% of all such deaths worldwide (1). Meanwhile, 2 of 3 people in the region cannot obtain the care they need, and 1 in 5 cuts spending on food or education to pay for health care (1). The first resolution (EM/RC73/R.3) tackles inadequate financial protection that pushes millions of people into hardship when they seek care. The second (EM/ RC73/R.4) seeks to replace the fragmented approaches to disease elimination, which leave millions vulnerable to preventable illness and death. Both resolutions demand changes to how countries invest in health, organize services and use available resources. None of the resolutions can stop a war or end a humanitarian crisis, but both can change what happens when someone needs medical care: whether treatment pushes a family into poverty, or an infection is detected before it spreads, or health system protects those most at- risk. This is what makes implementation very important. Protecting people from the cost of care No family should have to choose between treating an illness and keeping a roof over its head. However, across the EMR, around 28% of people experience financial hardship due to health spending, and nearly 4 in 5 of those affected must forgo basic needs to obtain care (3). These are not simply financing problems. They are failures of financial protection, with consequences for health, household welfare and economic security. Governments fund only 48% of current health care expenditure, against 53% globally, and in the region’s low-income countries households pay 61% of health care costs out of pocket (3). At the same time, inefficient spending compounds the problem. WHO estimates that 20–40% of health spending is lost to inefficiency, through fragmented financing pools, inadequate regulation of the private sector, poorly designed payment systems, and overreliance on hospitals (3). Countries must therefore spend more on health, but they must also spend better. Resolution EM/RC73/R.3 calls for increased public financing, more equitable prepayment and pooling arrangements, strategic purchasing, closer links between health financing and social protection, and financing systems that can respond to crises, including through Islamic social financing (4). There is already progress to build on. Egypt is implementing universal health insurance, Pakistan is expanding its Sehat Sahulat Programme, Lebanon is using health taxes to create fiscal space, and Sudan is pooling procurement of high-cost medicines. Bahrain, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are extending mandatory health insurance for their large expatriate populations (3). However, isolated reforms will not deliver Universal Health Coverage. Ministries of health and ministries of finance must work together to develop costed strategies backed by medium-term budgets, with greater investment in primary health care and financial protection for all. WHO will support these efforts through the regional Health Financing Taskforce (4). Disease elimination requires integration The case for a more integrated approach to communicable diseases is equally compelling. In 2023, communicable diseases accounted for more than 8 million disability- adjusted life years in the EMR, and the burden of some diseases is increasing (5). Nearly 28 million people live with chronic hepatitis B or C (6) and an estimated 78 million people still require interventions against neglected tropical diseases in the region (7). Malaria incidence more than doubled between 2015 and 2024, from 9.0 to 19.1 cases per 1000 population (5). And only 660 Editorial EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 10 – 2026 28% of the 610 000 people living with HIV receive treatment (5). Many EMR countries continue to tackle individual diseases through separate programmes, each with its own surveillance, laboratory, procurement, and reporting systems. These arrangements duplicate efforts, stretch scarce resources and miss opportunities to reach people with multiple health needs. Resolution EM/RC73/R.2 seeks to change this by advancing an integrated approach to eliminating 14 priority communicable diseases. It calls for shared surveillance, diagnostics, procurement, and primary health care delivery, while preserving the specialised expertise needed to tackle individual diseases (5,8). Integration does not mean abandoning disease- specific programmes; it means making them work together. There is evidence that this approach delivers results. Oman eliminated mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis in 2022 through integrated maternal and child health services. And every US$ 1 invested in integrated neglected tropical disease interventions is estimated to generate around US$ 25 in returns (5). Integration and collaboration must extend beyond national borders. The 2022 devastating floods in Pakistan contributed to an estimated 6.6 million additional malaria cases and were linked to renewed local transmission in Islamic Republic of Iran (5). Along the Red Sea rim, Djibouti, Somalia, Sudan, and Yemen face overlapping disease threats that demand stronger cross-border cooperation (5). WHO will support countries through a regional implementation framework, measurable milestones and an investment case for integrated elimination (5,8). The challenge now is to translate these commitments into coordinated action at country level. Gains under pressure The EMR has demonstrated that sustained investment and coordinated action can deliver major public health gains. Nine countries have eliminated trachoma as a public health problem; most recently Egypt, Libya and Tunisia (5). Even in conflict-affected Sudan, coverage with the third dose of pentavalent vaccine increased from 38% in 2024 to 71% in 2025 (1). However, these achievements are fragile. In 2025, 2.4 million children in the EMR received no routine vaccines, an improvement on the 2024 achievement, but above the 2.1 million recorded in 2019 (9). Wild poliovirus transmission in Afghanistan and Pakistan has declined since peaking in 2024, but it persists in Karachi, southern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and southern Afghanistan. Reaching every missed child during the coming low-transmission season will be critical to interrupting the remaining chains of transmission (9,10). These challenges are unfolding as resources become increasingly constrained. WHO’s base programme budget for the region was reduced by 14% for 2026–2027 (11), and the regional office has cut more than 300 staff positions (1). As of the end of June 2026, more than 40% of WHO’s emergency response requirements for the EMR remained unfunded (1). Countries must make better use of available resources, but efficiency cannot substitute for adequate, predictable financing, particularly in settings affected by conflict and displacement. International partners must also align their support with national priorities, strengthen country systems and channel their funding through national budgets wherever possible (3). Questions Regional Committee 74 should answer When the Regional Committee meets for its 74th Session in October 2027, household data would not have shown the impact of these decisions: the latest regional estimates of financial hardship are for 2022 (3). The test would be the earlier signals. Have ministries of finance backed costed health financing strategies in their budgets? Are countries rolling out integrated multi- disease elimination plans that target people previously missed, including those displaced across borders? Has the low-transmission season cut wild poliovirus circulation in its last reservoirs? If we cannot answer yes within a year, we would have mistaken agreement for progress. By RC74, countries must be able to demonstrate that these decisions are beginning to change how health care is financed, how services are delivered and, ultimately, what happens to people when they need health care. analysis.summary_en: This paper examines the health care changes proposed following the 73rd Session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR). It highlights the region's significant health needs, including disease outbreaks and financial barriers to care, and discusses the two resolutions aimed at improving financial protection and integrating disease elimination strategies. The study emphasizes the importance of policy implementation and collaboration between health and finance ministries to address these challenges. While the findings suggest the potential for public health improvements through better financing and integrated approaches, the evidence is based on policy documents and aggregated data, which may limit the depth of analysis. The study underscores the need for more equitable health spending and coordinated action to tackle communicable diseases and enhance health system resilience in the EMR.
